references.text: God reveals himself as the one who forgives sin and guilt. The scribes claimed that only God can forgive sins, and this Old Testament passage confirms that forgiveness belongs to God's nature.
The Lord declares that it is he, and he alone, who blots out transgressions. This supports the scribes' statement that only God can forgive sins.
God says that he has blotted out transgressions like a cloud. Once again it is emphasized that forgiveness of sin is God's sovereign right, as the scribes pointed out.
The psalmist praises the Lord who forgives all guilt. This shows that forgiveness of sin is a divine privilege, which the scribes referred to.
With the Lord there is forgiveness, so that he may be feared. Forgiveness is God's own domain, which made Jesus' statement controversial in the eyes of the scribes.
With our God the Lord there is mercy and forgiveness. Once again it is confirmed that forgiveness belongs to God, which the scribes used as grounds for their accusation of blasphemy.
The parallel passage in Mark where the scribes think in their hearts that Jesus is blaspheming God because he forgives sins, since only God can do so.
The parallel passage in Matthew where some of the scribes thought that Jesus was blaspheming God by pronouncing forgiveness of sins.
The Jews wanted to stone Jesus for blasphemy because he, being a man, made himself out to be God. The same type of accusation as here in Luke 5:21.
Later in Luke, the guests at the table raise the same question: "Who is this who even forgives sins?" – the same reaction as the scribes here.
The law stipulates that whoever blasphemes the name of the Lord shall die. The scribes' accusation of blasphemy therefore amounted to a serious charge with the death penalty as a consequence.
